draft.title: The Iron Curtain and Europe divided
card: After the war Soviet forces held much of eastern Europe. Communist governments, backed by the Soviet Union, took power in countries such as Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia.
In 1946 Winston Churchill said an "iron curtain" had come down across Europe. The phrase described the split between the Soviet-controlled east and the western countries.
Germany was divided into four zones run by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. Berlin lay inside the Soviet zone but was also split into four sectors.
In 1949 the western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone became East Germany. Europe now had two opposing blocs.
draft.remember: Europe split into a Soviet east and a western bloc, and Germany and Berlin were divided too.

a.q: What did the phrase "iron curtain" describe?
opts: The split between Soviet-controlled east and the west
A wall built around the city of Berlin
A treaty ending the war in Europe
The border between Germany and Poland
a.why: Churchill used the phrase for the division of Europe into east and west. It was not a physical wall around Berlin, which is the tempting wrong answer.
a.clue: It was a way of speaking about the whole continent.

b.q: Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone of Germany. How was the city governed after the war?
opts: Split into four sectors run by the four powers
Run wholly by the Soviet Union as its capital
Run by Britain alone as a neutral city
Split in two, with the west of Berlin under Germany
b.why: Berlin was divided into four sectors, even though it lay inside the Soviet zone. It was not under Soviet control alone, which is tempting because of where it was.
b.clue: Berlin copied the way Germany itself was divided.

a.best: The split between Soviet-controlled east and the west

b.best: Split into four sectors run by the four powers

problems.detail: The right option is clearly the longest and repeats the card's wording almost word for word ('Soviet-controlled east'), so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

proposal.title: The Iron Curtain and Europe divided
card: After the war Soviet forces held much of eastern Europe. Communist governments, backed by the Soviet Union, took power in countries such as Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia.

In 1946 Winston Churchill said an "iron curtain" had come down across Europe. It was a figure of speech, not a real barrier, for the split between the communist, Soviet-controlled east and the western countries.
Germany was divided into four zones run by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union. Berlin lay inside the Soviet zone but was also split into four sectors.
In 1949 the western zones became West Germany and the Soviet zone became East Germany. Europe now had two opposing blocs.
proposal.remember: Europe split into a Soviet east and a western bloc, and Germany and Berlin were divided too.

a.q: In his 1946 speech, what was Churchill describing with the words "iron curtain"?
opts: A divide between Europe's communist east and its west
A concrete wall built through the middle of Berlin
A peace treaty that ended the war in Europe in 1945
A trade ban the west placed on the Soviet Union
a.why: Churchill used the phrase as a figure of speech for the division of Europe into a communist east and a western bloc. It was not a real wall in Berlin, which is the tempting answer because a wall was built there years later.
a.clue: Churchill was speaking about the whole continent, not one city.

b.q: Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone of Germany. How was the city governed after the war?
opts: Split into four sectors run by the four powers
Run wholly by the Soviet Union as its capital
Run by Britain alone as a neutral city
Split in two, with the west of Berlin under Germany
b.why: Berlin was divided into four sectors, even though it lay inside the Soviet zone. It was not under Soviet control alone, which is tempting because of where it was.
b.clue: Berlin copied the way Germany itself was divided.
